visits.text: There’s nothing natural here, and that’s deliberate: Gardens by the Bay opened in 2012 on land reclaimed from the sea, covering 101 hectares right in the city center. Supertree Grove is its heart: eighteen artificial trees, 25 to 50 meters tall, covered in climbing plants. Admission to the outdoor park is free; only the conservatories and elevated walkways require tickets.

Cool, damp air hits you as soon as you enter Cloud Forest, a chilled conservatory that recreates a tropical mountain. An indoor waterfall more than thirty meters high towers over the entrance, and the route spirals up to the summit before descending along an elevated walkway. Allow a full hour and bring a light layer; it’s considerably cooler inside than outside.

Flower Dome is worth a visit even if conservatories aren’t your thing: this cool, dry glasshouse brings together plants from five continents across 1.28 hectares and has held the Guinness World Record for the largest glass greenhouse since 2015. The displays change with the seasons. Visit it before Cloud Forest; the climate transition is easier in that order.

If heights don’t bother you, the OCBC Skyway connects two Supertrees with an elevated walkway suspended above the park. The loop is short, with views across the bay and the business district. It requires a separate ticket from the conservatories, and late-afternoon time slots fill up first.

activities.text: Unabashedly kitschy, but Garden Rhapsody works: every evening, the Supertrees light up in sync with a soundtrack above spectators lying on the grass. The show is free and lasts a few minutes, with two evening performances. Arrive ten minutes early and lie right down on the ground for the best view.

Continue to World of Plants, a series of outdoor themed gardens at the back of the park, free and almost empty when the conservatories are packed. Explore tropical plants by habitat: forest understory, carnivorous plants, and palms. Go early in the morning or after 5 p.m.; there is almost no shade in between.

visits.text: A fifteen-minute boat ride away, Pulau Ubin resembles the Singapore of old: wooden houses, dirt tracks and wild boars roaming freely. The island covers just over a thousand hectares. There is no ATM, so get cash before boarding.

Chek Jawa was scheduled to be reclaimed in 2001. Saved at the last minute, this wetland brings together six habitats across roughly a hundred hectares: sandy beach, rocky intertidal zone, seagrass meadow, coral rubble, mangrove, and coastal forest. Two wooden elevated walkways, the 600-meter coastal loop and the 500-meter mangrove loop, let you see everything without getting wet. Open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Climb the twenty-one meters of Jejawi Tower, an observation tower set in Chek Jawa’s coastal forest. From the top, you can see the mangrove on one side and the Strait of Johor on the other, with Malaysia across the water. The climb is steep and unshaded, so save it for early morning.

At Chek Jawa, the coastal boardwalk lets you observe the shore without stepping onto the intertidal zone. At low tide, look for crabs and small creatures among the rocks, then continue along the mangrove loop among the aerial roots. Stay on the boardwalks to protect these fragile habitats and keep your bags closed if monkeys approach.

activities.text: If you arrive early, the bumboat gets underway sooner: boats leave Changi Point Ferry Terminal on no fixed schedule, only once twelve passengers are aboard. Expect to pay a few dollars per person each way, with an extra charge for a bicycle. The last return boat leaves in the early evening, so don’t miss it.

Cycling remains the best way to explore Pulau Ubin: rental shops are clustered in the village by the landing, and Chek Jawa is three kilometers away. Check the brakes before setting off, as the condition of the rental bikes varies widely. Bicycles are not allowed on the elevated walkways, so leave yours at the entrance.

Oriental pied hornbills had disappeared from Singapore; the ones seen at Chek Jawa today descend from birds that returned from Johor in the 1990s. Artificial nest boxes have been installed along the trails. Come early: you’ll hear them long before you see them.

visits.text: A leisure island built on a grim past, Sentosa was once called Pulau Blakang Mati, “the island behind which lies death.” A British military base and then a prisoner camp during the Japanese occupation, it was renamed in the 1970s to become a beach resort. You can reach it by monorail, pedestrian bridge, or cable car.

Explore cannons, casemates, and three tunnel networks at your own pace at Fort Siloso, Singapore’s only surviving coastal fort. Construction began in 1878, and it was designated a national monument in 2022. Admission is free. Bring water: the site is on a slope, and a visit involves a good hour of walking.

Reach the fort via the Fort Siloso Skywalk, a 181-meter suspended elevated walkway accessed by elevator from the bottom of the hill. The view looks down over the canopy and the strait crowded with cargo ships. It is also the only way to reach the fort without walking uphill.

Siloso Beach is artificial, and it shows: imported sand, cargo ships on the horizon, and bars lined up behind the palms. It is still the liveliest of the island’s three beaches, with lifeguards on duty. Come on a weekday; on weekends, groups fill the beach and the music gets louder.

Singapore Oceanarium, formerly S.E.A. Aquarium, can be visited within the Resorts World Sentosa complex. Its large panoramic tank lets you watch rays passing just centimeters from the glass. Explore the areas devoted to marine environments and book your ticket before visiting.

activities.text: If you are traveling with children, Universal Studios Singapore can easily fill half a day within the Resorts World Sentosa complex. The park is compact, which means less walking but more concentrated lines. Buy your ticket online the day before and arrive when the park opens; the difference in wait times is huge.

The ground drops away beneath your feet as soon as your Singapore Cable Car cabin leaves Mount Faber. Operating since 1974, the line passes over Keppel Harbour before reaching Sentosa. The ride takes about ten minutes. Travel in this direction on your way there; the descent toward the island is more impressive than the reverse trip.

Take the Sentosa Express from VivoCity mall instead of a taxi: the monorail serves three stations on the island and avoids traffic jams on the bridge. On foot, the elevated walkway from VivoCity takes about fifteen minutes to cross, with shade and no admission charge. It is the easiest option if you arrive early.

visits.text: Touristy to an almost absurd degree, Merlion Park still delivers: this is where the bay suddenly opens up before you, with Marina Bay Sands opposite. The water-spouting lion is the city’s official symbol, and everyone takes the same photo here. Come before 8 AM or after 9 PM, or you’ll wait your turn behind thirty people.

Built in 1928 in a neoclassical style, the Fullerton Building served as Singapore’s main post office before becoming a hotel. Its main draw is the view from its steps: the best angle on Marina Bay Sands across the water. Stop by in the late afternoon, when the light hits the facade head-on.

The hot air shimmers above the Helix Bridge, whose steel double helix echoes the shape of DNA. The pedestrian bridge connects the Esplanade to Marina Bay Sands in just a few minutes, with viewing platforms along the way. Cross it at night: the colored lights come on, making the bridge far more photogenic than in full sunlight.

A dam turned into a park is a surprising idea: Marina Barrage closes off the bay to create a freshwater reservoir, and its green roof has become a kite-flying spot for Singaporean families. It offers unobstructed skyline views, away from the waterfront crowds. Bring water; there’s no shade up there.

If you pay for just one view, make it the Sands SkyPark, the terrace spanning the three towers of Marina Bay Sands. The observation deck overlooks the bay and the business district; the pool is reserved for hotel guests. Go up one hour before sunset to see the city by day and by night without paying again.

Step into a Singapore Flyer capsule if walking has worn you out: the observation wheel turns slowly above Marina Bay, and a full rotation takes about thirty minutes. The cabin is air-conditioned, which matters in this climate. Avoid midafternoon, when the heat haze swallows the horizon.

activities.text: Free yet impressive, the waterfront sound and light show takes place at Event Plaza, at the foot of Marina Bay Sands. Water jets, lasers, and projections onto a curtain of water fill about ten minutes, with several performances each evening. Stand on the promenade side rather than the shopping mall side for a much better viewing angle.

Walk the waterfront loop from the Marina Bay Sands shopping mall to Merlion Park via the Helix Bridge and Jubilee Bridge. Allow one to one and a half hours at an easy pace; the entire route is flat and pedestrian-only. Set out after 6 PM: the heat eases, and the facades light up one by one.

The wind and brackish water greet you as soon as the bumboat leaves the dock on the Singapore River. The boat passes the converted warehouses of Boat Quay and Clarke Quay before emerging into the bay, taking about forty minutes. Board at sunset: it’s the only time when the outward and return trips look different.

Cycling at night beats any sightseeing bus for exploring Marina Bay: guided rides leave in the evening and take in the promenade, the riverbanks, and Gardens by the Bay. The pace is slow, and there’s almost no traffic on the bike paths. Check the departure time; these tours only run in the evening.

visits.text: Singapore Botanic Gardens became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015, the first site in the country to receive that status. Founded in 1859, it covers 82 hectares and admission is free. Arrive before 9 a.m.: that is when you will find joggers, parakeets, and the only cool air of the day.

A thousand orchid species all at once can overwhelm the senses: the National Orchid Garden, opened in 1995, occupies the park’s highest hill. It also includes the VIP Orchid Garden, where hybrids are named after visiting heads of state. This is the only section of the gardens that charges admission; allow 1 hour.

A rare surviving Anglo-Malay-style plantation house, Burkill Hall overlooks the orchid garden and once served as the residence of the gardens’ directors. The interior is not open for unrestricted visits. Stick to the terrace: it overlooks Palm Valley and the forest patch.

To understand why these gardens matter, step into the Rain Forest: a remnant of tropical forest preserved in the middle of the city, older than the gardens themselves. The loop trail takes fifteen minutes. It gets slippery after rain, so closed-toe shoes are recommended.

activities.text: Enter through Tanglin Gate rather than Bukit Timah Gate: the gardens stretch 2.5 kilometers from north to south, and the historic section, with Swan Lake and the 1930s bandstand, is at this end. Walking the full length takes 1 hour. A bottle of water is no luxury.

A picnic on the Palm Valley lawn beats a sit-down lunch: this is where Singaporeans gather on weekends, sometimes for an outdoor concert performed on the floating stage. Buy food before entering; options inside are limited and expensive.
